Yet it is absent from most climate funding frameworks. Investing here is not only an equity issue but also an economic imperative." Learn more The results from our survey Our survey: midwives warn extreme heat is outpacing maternal care No pregnancy is complete without midwives and health professionals and yet their voices are often missing from the conversation on extreme heat and its impact on pregnancy. To address this, in September 2026, Censuswide conducted a survey of 1,000 currently practicing healthcare professionals - including 250 midwives - across the UK, India, Australia, Brazil and Zimbabwe, involved in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal or newborn care to understand their perceptions of how extreme heat impacts pregnant women and their babies. Their message is clear: health concerns linked to extreme heat are rising, but the guidance, training and facilities needed to protect pregnant women and babies have not kept pace. METHODOLOGY PRESS RELEASE See the results from our poll Health professionals are already seeing the impact 98% have personally cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believe was adversely affected by extreme heat. 99% have personally cared for a baby whose health they believe was adversely affected by extreme heat. 73% report an increase in heat-related cases or complications related to extreme heat affecting pregnant women. 76% report an increase in heat-related cases or complications affecting foetal or newborn health in the past five years. 81% are concerned that extreme heat will pose a growing risk to maternal, foetal and newborn health over the next five years unless further action is taken. 92% want more training and resources to protect pregnant women during extreme heat. 82% believe policymakers and health-system leaders should give greater priority to protecting pregnant women and babies from extreme heat. Solutions exist The evidence justifies action. ‍ Communities that have long lived with extreme heat are already developing and testing practical ways to protect pregnant women and babies. These include heat alerts, health-worker training, income protection, cooling measures and adaptations to health facilities. Organisations like Wellcome are helping to build the evidence base and solutions are already being piloted, from the UK to India to Zimbabwe. Learn more Australia: learn more about the heat and pregnancy study Australia Australia has a diverse climate and population which provides a unique opportunity to understand the impact of extreme heat exposure during pregnancy. Learn more Brazil: learn more about CIDACS Climate work on heat & pregnancy Brazil In Brazil, Wellcome is funding the Center for Data Integration and Knowledge in Health (CIDACS) - Clima Climate and Health Data study to conduct research on heat and pregnancy. Learn more Zimbabwe & South Africa ‍ Temperatures in Southern Africa are rising at twice the global rate, with major health implications for maternal and newborn health. Those in Zimbabwe are at particular risk due to socio-economic challenges and their limited access to cooling resources. The HAPI Study (Heat Adaptation for Pregnant Women and Infants), led by Professor Matthew Chersich and funded by Wellcome, explores a range of protective mechanisms, including behavioural, built environment, and environmental innovations. The study will work with 1600 women across six maternity facilities and their surrounding communities and households in in urban Tshwane, South Africa, and rural Mount Darwin District, Zimbabwe. These areas have contrasting climatic conditions, economies and socio-cultural practices. The key interventions studied include: Behavioural strategies to improve hydration and mitigate heat exposure. Built environment modifications, including ventilation and cooling designs. Community-focused education and engagement to enhance awareness and resilience. The study aims to identify scalable interventions to reduce heat-related health risks for pregnant women and infants. Early findings suggest that low-cost measures, including water bottles, rechargeable fans, heat-health information and reflective roof paint in health facilities, can help protect women and babies. The programme is also testing community-led approaches through Heat Champions, cooling hubs and tree planting. As temperatures continue to rise, hundreds of millions of pregnant women are becoming more exposed - and the burden falls hardest on those with the fewest resources to adapt. Stories from women and mothers around the world These are personal accounts from women and frontline health workers showing us what extreme heat means in practice. Fortunate Machingura Director of Climate, Environment and Health, CeSHHAR Zimbabwe "The challenge is still just basic understanding of the impacts of heat on pregnancy. We see lower birth weight, we see prolonged labour in the antepartum phase, but we also see preterm birth – children coming much earlier than their time. And it’s because of this labour in the heat." Learn more Rutendo Mhandu HAPI heat champion Zimbabwe "Heat affects the health of pregnant women. They may deliver a stillbirth or a lightweight baby – some of the things that I have heard happened to pregnant women because of heat. They swell, the legs swell, they get dizzy and they also give birth to preterm babies, and babies that are not very healthy." Skip Link Intro Stats Survey Case Studies Action Digital Toolkit Extreme heat is putting pregnant women and their babies at risk We must act now Extreme heat is now one of the most immediate and visible health impacts of climate change. Yet the risks it poses to pregnant women and newborns remain largely absent from climate adaptation, health policy and emergency planning. Learn more Extreme heat is linked to premature birth, low birth weight, stillbirth and maternal complications. Those least able to avoid exposure or adapt their homes and working conditions face the greatest risks. Pregnant women and babies remain overlooked in many heat-health responses. Governments, international organisations and health systems must act now to protect them and build healthier, more resilient communities in a warming world. A 2026 survey of healthcare professionals To understand how extreme heat is affecting maternal and newborn health, Wellcome commissioned a survey of 1,000 healthcare professionals working in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal and newborn care across Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe. The findings reveal widespread concern. 73% reported that heat-linked cases of complications have increased over the past five years. 81% are concerned that, without action, extreme heat will pose a growing risk to maternal, foetal and newborn health. 98% had cared for a woman or baby whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat. 92% want more training, guidance and resources to help protect pregnant women during pregnancy. The impacts of heat are not felt equally Women who cannot avoid exposure to extreme heat, because of their jobs or living conditions, often face the greatest risks. But solutions do exist. About 66% of Indian clinicians reported a rise in heat-related complications affecting foetuses or newborns, while 62% reported an increase among pregnant women. The Wellcome study surveyed 1,000 healthcare professionals across India, the UK, Australia, Brazil and Zimbabwe, with 200 respondents in each country. Clinicians reported suspected heat-related impacts including low birth weight, restricted foetal growth, dehydration and feeding difficulties among newborns. At COP31, a UN climate official warned that only about 1% of formal climate finance goes to health, calling for greater investment in climate-resilient healthcare systems. Nearly all Indian healthcare professionals surveyed in a new global study reported treating pregnant women and newborns whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat, highlighting growing concerns over the impact of climate change on maternal and infant health. The study, presented by global health research organisation Wellcome on November 13 on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, surveyed 1,000 healthcare professionals across five countries. In India, 98 per cent of respondents said they had cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believed was affected by extreme heat, according to a media briefing. The same proportion reported treating a baby affected by heat. The findings were presented in the presence of senior UN climate officials, who acknowledged that health receives only a small share of international climate finance. India reports widespread heat-related health impacts According to the study, 66 per cent of Indian respondents reported an increase in heat-related cases or complications affecting foetal or newborn health over the past five years, while 62 per cent reported an increase in complications affecting pregnant women. More than a quarter (26 per cent) said they had encountered pregnancy complications requiring additional monitoring or treatment. Clinicians described a range of suspected heat-related effects, including low birth weight, restricted foetal growth, dehydration and feeding difficulties among newborns. The survey was conducted in September and October 2026 among 1,000 healthcare professionals in India, the UK, Australia, Brazil and Zimbabwe, with 200 respondents from each country. Participants included obstetricians, gynaecologists and frontline healthcare workers involved in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal and newborn care. Across the five countries, 73 per cent reported an increase in heat-related cases or complications affecting pregnant women over the previous five years, while 76 per cent reported an increase affecting foetal or newborn health. “Women exposed to extreme heat during pregnancy have much worse pregnancy outcomes: increased risk of stillbirth, pre-term birth and congenital abnormalities,” said Alan Dangour, Wellcome's director of climate and health, as per the briefing statement. “As the climate changes, this is going to become worse and worse. We are at the early stages now and must put in place the procedures, the guidelines and the systems to respond to this challenge,” he added. Health receives just 1 per cent of climate finance, says UN official Speaking at the launch, Youssef Nassef, director of the adaptation programme at UN Climate Change, acknowledged the limited funding available to address climate-related health risks. “Heat in particular has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies,” he said, adding that approximately 1 per cent of formal climate finance goes to health. Nassef said health was becoming increasingly important in international climate adaptation negotiations. He outlined three priorities under the Global Goal on Adaptation: preventing climate-related deaths and illness, strengthening the resilience of healthcare systems, and helping communities adapt to the health impacts of climate change. He called for assessments at national and subnational levels to identify gaps in healthcare preparedness and estimate the funding needed to address them. “Once that is concluded and countries have started working on this now, piloting the use of the indicators for the global goal, then we can start calculating where we are versus where we need to be,” he said. “I suspect that the amount of funding needed will be a lot more than 1 per cent.” Nassef also argued that health policies must account for envi
